Response to constant daily training

Source: R/banister-responses.R
constant_training.Rd

Computes fitness, fatigue and predicted performance when the same load is done every day from day 1, with the closed forms of Morton et al. (1990, Eqs. 6, 9-11), the asymptote of predicted performance and the day of poorest performance (MODELS.md, M-04). Nothing is fitted: the parameters are given by the user. The initial state is 0.

Usage

constant_training(
  load,
  k1,
  tau1,
  k2 = NULL,
  tau2 = NULL,
  p0 = 0,
  model = c("two_component", "fitness_only"),
  days = 100,
  same_day_load = c("exclude", "include")
)

Arguments

load

Daily training load, a single finite number > 0, done every day from day 1.

k1

Gain of fitness, a single finite number >= 0.

tau1

Time constant of fitness in days, a single finite number > 0. Arguments are time constants, never half-lives (D-024): see time_constant() to convert a half-life.

k2

Gain of fatigue, a single finite number >= 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

tau2

Time constant of fatigue in days, a single finite number > 0. Required for the two-component model; must not be given for the fitness-only model.

p0

Baseline performance, a single finite number.

model

"two_component" (the default; fitness and fatigue) or "fitness_only" (D-023).

days

Last day of the curve, a single whole number >= 1.

same_day_load

Timing convention: "exclude" (the default) or "include". See the section on the timing convention.

Value

A list of class "constant_training" with the elements

  • curve: a data frame with the columns day (1 to days), fitness, fatigue (NA for the fitness-only model) and predicted;

  • asymptote: predicted performance as days grow;

  • time_of_minimum: day of poorest performance, or NA;

  • load, model, same_day_load, days and parameters: the arguments used.

Formula

For a daily load \(T\) and the time constant \(\tau\) of either component, $$g_{inc}(t) = T\,\frac{1 - e^{-t/\tau}}{1 - e^{-1/\tau}}, \qquad g_{exc}(t) = T\,e^{-1/\tau}\,\frac{1 - e^{-(t-1)/\tau}}{1 - e^{-1/\tau}}$$ under same_day_load = "include" and "exclude" (the default, D-012). These equal simulate_banister() on a series of constant load.

Asymptote

The asymptote is the predicted performance as days grow. It depends on the convention: since \(g_{exc}(t) = g_{inc}(t) - T\), the "exclude" asymptote is the "include" one minus \((k_1 - k_2)\,T\): $$p_{inc}(\infty) = p_0 + \frac{k_1 T}{1 - e^{-1/\tau_1}} - \frac{k_2 T}{1 - e^{-1/\tau_2}}, \qquad p_{exc}(\infty) = p_0 + \frac{k_1 T e^{-1/\tau_1}}{1 - e^{-1/\tau_1}} - \frac{k_2 T e^{-1/\tau_2}}{1 - e^{-1/\tau_2}}.$$

Time of minimum

The day of poorest performance (Morton et al. 1990, Eq. 10; their \(t_n\), named in words here, D-026) is $$\mathrm{time\_of\_minimum} = \frac{\tau_1 \tau_2}{\tau_1 - \tau_2} \ln\frac{\tau_1 k_2 (1 - e^{-1/\tau_1})}{\tau_2 k_1 (1 - e^{-1/\tau_2})},$$ the same under both conventions. It is a continuous time: the day with the lowest predicted value in curve is the nearest whole day.

time_of_minimum is NA when there is no minimum: when \(\tau_1 \le \tau_2\), when the argument of the logarithm is \(\le 1\) (fatigue is too small for performance to dip), when \(k_1 = 0\) (performance only falls), and for the fitness-only model (performance only rises).

References

Morton RH, Fitz-Clarke JR, Banister EW (1990). Modeling human performance in running. Journal of Applied Physiology, 69(3), 1171-1177.

See also

simulate_banister(), session_response(), half_life().

Examples

# Morton et al. (1990): load 100 every day
constant_training(100, k1 = 1, tau1 = 45, k2 = 2, tau2 = 15,
                  same_day_load = "include")
#> <constant_training> Constant daily training of 100: two-component model
#> Timing convention: same_day_load = "include" (a day's load counts on the same day)
#> Parameters: p0 = 0, k1 = 1, k2 = 2
#> Time constants: tau1 = 45 days (half-life 31.19 days), tau2 = 15 days (half-life 10.4 days)
#> Asymptote of predicted performance: 1449.07
#> Time of minimum: 16.09 days
#> Curve: days 1 to 100 in $curve.
